INTEREST OF THE AMICUS CURIAE1
Amicus curiae America’s Future is a nonstock,
nonprofit organization, exempt from federal income
taxation under section 501(c)(3) of the Internal
Revenue Code.  It is dedicated, inter alia, to the correct
construction, interpretation, and application of law.
This amicus participates actively in the public policy
process and has filed numerous amicus curiae briefs in
federal and state courts, including 12 in this Court
over the last two years supporting Applications for
stays of district court injunctions issued to stop policy
changes by the second Trump Administration.
This amicus filed amicus briefs in this case in this
Court supporting the Government’s two applications
for stay.  See U.S. Supreme Court Docket No. 24A1153,
Brief Amicus Curiae of America’s Future, et al. in
Support of Application for Stay (June 5, 2025) and
Docket No. 26A406, Brief Amicus Curiae of America’s
Future in Support of Application for Stay (September
28, 2026).
STATEMENT OF THE CASE
This amicus offers the following rather detailed
Statement of the Case in an effort to demonstrate how
extraordinary the actions of one federal district court,
and the First Circuit, have been.  A review of how this
district court has attempted to control the enforcement
1  It is hereby certified that no counsel for a party authored this
brief in whole or in part; and that no person other than this
amicus curiae, its members, or its counsel made a monetary
contribution to its preparation or submission.

2
of immigration laws and the conduct of our nation’s
foreign policy will speak as loudly as any argument
that could be made as to why Congress denied to the
district courts the very powers which this district court
has exercised.
On January 20, 2025, President Trump issued
Executive Order 14165, entitled “Securing Our
Borders,” reversing policies of the Biden
Administration.  See 90 Fed. Reg. 8467.  On or about
February 18, 2025, the Department of Homeland
Security (“DHS”) issued a Directive to the Enforcement
and Removal Operations (“ERO”) division of
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (“ICE”).  That
Directive instructed ERO officers to review the cases
of aliens granted withholding of removal or protection
under the Convention Against Torture (“CAT”) to
determine the availability of removal to a third
country.  In  the case of aliens under prior orders of
removal who could not be removed because the
countries designated in removal orders were unwilling
to take them, ERO addressed how they would be
removed instead to “third countries,” i.e., countries not
named on the initial removal order, as permitted by
law.
On March 23, 2025, four illegal aliens filed suit in
the district court for the District of Massachusetts,
seeking a temporary restraining order (“TRO”) and
other injunctive relief against the Directive.  See
D.V.D. v. United States Dep’t of Homeland Sec., 2025
U.S. Dist. LEXIS 59422 at *2 (D. Mass. 2025) (“D.V.D.
I ”).  The district court considered two claims for relief
— one under CAT and one under 8 U.S.C.

3
§ 1231(b)(3)(A), which states, “the Attorney General
may not remove an alien to a country if the Attorney
General decides that the alien’s life or freedom
would be threatened in that country....” (Emphasis
added.)
On March 28, 2025, the district court issued a TRO
on statutory claims limited to the named plaintiffs,
which was followed by issuance of a Memorandum
Opinion on March 29, 2025.  However, the TRO on
CAT claims was not limited to the named plaintiffs,
but was made applicable to “all similarly situated
individuals.”  D.V.D. I at *9 (emphasis added).  The
district court cursorily rejected the Government’s
challenge to the court’s jurisdiction based on multiplee
statutes constraining federal court involvement,
including the following.  See id. at *3.
• 8 U.S.C. § 1252(g) states:  “Except as provided
in this section ... no court shall have
jurisdiction to hear any cause or claim by or
on behalf of any alien....”  (Emphasis added.)
• 8 U.S.C. § 1252(a)(5) states:  “a petition for
review filed with an appropriate court of
appeals in accordance with this section shall
be the sole and exclusive means for
judicial review of an order of removal
entered or issued under any provision of this
chapter.”  (Emphasis added.)
• 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(9) states:  “Except as
otherwise provided in this section, no court
shall have jurisdiction, by habeas corpus
under section 2241 of title 28 or any other
habeas corpus provision, by section 1361 or

4
1651 of such title, or by any other provision of
law (statutory or nonstatutory), to review
such an order....”  (Emphasis added.)
The district court declared that the threatened
removals did not actually constitute “orders of
removal” because some of the illegal aliens might not
be sent to countries listed as destinations on their
original removal orders, but to “third countries”
instead — even though removal to third countries is
authorized by law.  D.V.D. I at *3, *5.
The Government sought a stay from the First
Circuit, which was denied for the curious reason that
the circuit court simply did not know whether it had
jurisdiction to stay the district court’s TRO.  See
D.V.D. v. United States Dep’t of Homeland Sec., 2025
U.S. App. LEXIS 8338 (1st Cir. 2025) (“D.V.D. II”).
On April 18, 2025, the district court entered a
preliminary injunction against the Directive on the
assumption that the statutes barring judicial review
would not apply if the removals were unlawful on the
merits.  The court stated that “this Court will not
construe section 1252(g) to immunize an unlawful
practice from judicial review....  What Plaintiffs
challenge is Defendants’ authority to effectively depart
from the removal orders by designating new countries
for removal....”  D.V.D. v. United States Dep’t of
Homeland Sec., 778 F. Supp. 3d 355, 377 (D. Mass.
2025) (“D.V.D. III”).  The court’s theory to evade
limitations on its power was that if the removals were
viewed as illegal by the court, that would deprive DHS
of their authority to act, and “section 1252(g) shields

5
only discretionary decisions concerning ... the
deportation process.”  Id.  The district court granted a
sweeping preliminary injunction to institute and
implement what the court believed to be better
than the procedures established by Congress and the
Department of Homeland Security.  The district court
ordered the Government to follow procedures it
preferred:
[P]rior to removing any alien to a third
country, i.e., any country not explicitly
provided for on the alien’s order of removal,
Defendants must:  (1) provide written notice to
the alien — and the alien’s immigration
counsel, if any — of the third country to which
the alien may be removed...; (2) provide
meaningful opportunity for the alien to raise a
fear of return for eligibility for CAT
protections; (3) move to reopen the proceedings
if the alien demonstrates “reasonable fear”;
and (4) if the alien is not found to have
demonstrated “reasonable fear,” provide
meaningful opportunity, and a minimum of 15
days, for that alien to seek to move to reopen
immigration proceedings.  [Id. at 392-93.]
The district court then went even further and
certified a class of all persons subject to a final
removal order who DHS proposed to transfer to a
“third country” not listed on their original removal
order.  Id. at 378, 386.  Through this device, the
district court apparently believed it was authorized to
issue what was effectively a nationwide injunction —
a power which was denied to district courts later by

6
this Court’s June 27, 2025 decision in Trump v. CASA,
Inc., 606 U.S. 831 (2025).
On April 30, 2025, the district court extended its
April 18, 2025 preliminary injunction to apply to all
federal agencies, and on May 7, 2025, the district court
entered another order, styled by the court as a
“clarification,” prohibiting DHS from allowing other
agencies to perform the removals the court had
enjoined DHS from effectuating.  D.V.D. v. United
States Dep’t of Homeland Sec., 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS
88472 (D. Mass. 2025).  On May 16, 2025, the First
Circuit denied the Government’s emergency motion for
a stay of the April 18, 2025 preliminary injunction.2
On May 20, 2025, the district court entered
another order with respect to several individuals who
had been transported to South Sudan.  The order
directed DHS to “maintain custody and control of class
members currently being removed to South Sudan or
to any other third country, to ensure the practical
feasibility of return if the Court finds that such
removals were unlawful.”  D.V.D. v. United States
Dep’t of Homeland Sec., 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 98733,
*4 (D. Mass. 2025).
On May 21, 2025, the district court acted again to
“clarify” its D.V.D. III order for “‘meaningful
opportunity’” for an alien to raise fear of return for
CAT purposes.  The court ruled that “a minimum of
2 D.V.D. v. United States Dep’t of Homeland Sec., No. 25-1393,
“Order of Court,” Dkt. 00108286763 (May 16, 2025).

7
ten days” was required as “meaningful opportunity”
as a matter of due process.  D.V.D. v. United States
Dep’t of Homeland Sec., 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 98774
at *3 (D. Mass. 2025).
On May 23, 2025, the district court ordered DHS
to return one plaintiff, O.C.G., who had already
been transferred to Mexico, and thence home to
Guatemala.  D.V.D. v. United States Dep’t of Homeland
Sec., 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 99236 (D. Mass. 2025).
On May 26, 2025, the district court denied the
Government’s motion for reconsideration and to stay
its preliminary injunction.  D.V.D. v. United States
Dep’t of Homeland Sec., 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 99230
(D. Mass. 2025).  The following day, the Government
filed in this Court their first Application for Stay,
which was granted.3
In the evening of the same day that his
preliminary injunction was stayed by this Court,4
District Judge Murphy issued an order asserting that
its May remedial order “remains in full force and
effect, notwithstanding today’s [Supreme Court[
3  U.S. Supreme Court, No. 24A1153, “Application for a Stay of the
Injunction Issued by the United States District Court For the
District of Massachusetts and Request for an Immediate
Administrative Stay ” (May 27, 2025) (“App. Stay I”).
4  Dep’t of Homeland Sec. v. D.V.D., 145 S. Ct. 2153 (June 23,
2025).

8
stay of the Preliminary Injunction.”5  That required
DHS to file in this Court a “Motion to Clarify the
Court’s June 23, 2025 Order,”6 leading to a rare
“clarifying” ruling.
On June 23, we stayed the April 18
preliminary injunction pending disposition of
any appeal and petition for writ of certiorari.
Later that day, however, the District
Court issued a minute order stating that
the May 21 remedial order “remain[ed] in
full force and effect,” “notwithstanding”
our stay of the preliminary injunction....  The
only authority it cited was the dissent from the
stay order.  The Government has moved for

for clarification is granted.  Our June 23 order
stayed the April 18 preliminary injunction in
full.  The May 21 remedial order cannot now
be used to enforce an injunction that our stay
rendered unenforceable....  [A] claim that a
lower court has failed to give effect to an
order of this Court is properly addressed
here....  “Assuming as we do” that the District

Electronic order ofJudge Bryan e. Murphy (June 23, 2025)
(emphasis added).
6  U.S. Supreme Court, No. 24A1153, “Motion for an Order
Clarifying this Court’s June 23, 2025, Order Granting a Stay of
the Injunction Issued by the United States District Court for the
District of Massachusetts and Request for an Immediate

9
Court will now conform its order to our
previous stay and cease enforcing the April 18
injunction through the May 21 remedial order,
we have no occasion to reach the
Government’s other requests for relief....
If the Government wishes to seek additional
relief in aid of the execution of our mandate, it
may do so through mandamus.  [Dep’t of
Homeland Sec. v. D.V.D., 145 S. Ct. 2627,
2629-30 (July 3, 2025) (emphasis added).]7
On February 3, 2026, the circuit court held oral
argument on DHS’s appeal of the preliminary
injunction, then on February 20, 2026, remanded for
dissolution of the preliminary injunction.8  On
February 25, 2026, the district court issued its final
judgment, granting Plaintiffs’ Motion for Summary
Judgment on Counts I and IV by imposing four
procedural requirements on the department’s removal
of class members, and declaring the “Third Country
Removal” policy “unlawful and SET[TING] ASIDE
that policy.”  D.V.D. v. United States Dep’t of
Homeland Sec., 821 F. Supp. 3d 102, 167-68 (D. Mass.
February 25, 2026) (“D.V.D. IV ”).
7   Between the two previous orders of this Court last summer, the
First Circuit dismissed an appeal from the TRO.  See D.V.D. v.
United States Dep’t of Homeland Sec., 2025 U.S. App. LEXIS
25000 (1st Cir. June 30, 2025).
8  D.V.D. v. United States Dep’t of Homeland Sec., 2026 U.S. App.
LEXIS 11895 (1st Cir. Feb. 20, 2026).

10
After oral argument on May 13, 2026, the First
Circuit issued its opinion on September 18, 2026,
stating:  “we vacate on standing grounds the two
declarations pertaining to DHS’s statutory obligation
to seek to remove class members to countries they
have designated, or of which they are subjects,
nationals, or citizens, prior to removing them to third
countries.  We otherwise affirm the final judgment.”
D.V.D. v. United States Dep’t of Homeland Sec., 2026
U.S. App. LEXIS 28742 at *51 (1st Cir. Sep. 18, 2026)
(“D.V.D. V ”) (all emphasis original).
Five days after the First Circuit’s decision, at 8:20
pm on September 23, 2026, the Plaintiffs-Appellees
filed an Emergency Motion in the circuit court,9 which
a panel granted three hours later, at 11:36 pm,
ordering that “the March 16, 2026, stay pending
appeal is dissolved.”10
The next day, on September 24, 2026, the
Government filed another Application for a Stay (“App.
Stay II”)11 in this Court, explaining that shockingly,
the First Circuit’s September 23 order had been issued
9  U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit, No. 26-1212,
“Emergency Motion to Clarify the Effectiveness of this Court’s
Decision or, In the Alternative, Confirm the Stay is Lifted or Issue
the Mandate” (Sept. 23, 2026).
10  U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit, No. 26-1212, “Order
of the Court” (Sept. 23, 2026).
11  The Government’s second filing in this Court was captioned not
as an application for stay, but rather as a Motion to Clarify.  See
n.6, supra.

11
without providing time for the Government to respond
(see App. Stay II at 2) as well as short-circuiting the
timeline for issuing a mandate under F.R.App.P.
40(d)(1), 41(b).  On September 29, 2026, this Court
stayed the February 25, 2026 order and judgment of
the district court, treated the application as a petition
for a writ of certiorari, and  granted it.
Discussed above are just a few of the many orders
issued by the district court as it sought to assume
control over DHS enforcement.  At no time, in any of
those orders and opinions, did the district court feel
obligated to give meaningful consideration to the
Government’s interest in removing persons illegally in
the United States, and discouraging other aliens from
similarly violating the law if they knew that if they
arrived illegally, they would be removed, to a third
country, if necessary.  Moreover, at no time did the
district court feel the need to give consideration to the
importance of protecting the American People from
those who had committed crimes in the United States,
and were likely to commit further crimes, including
sex offenses and murder.  See Brief for the Petitioners
(“Pet. Br.”) at 3 (“Criminal aliens — including class
members here who have been convicted of murder,
armed robbery, sexual assault of minors and the
mentally disabled, and more — have ravaged
American communities.”).  Despite clear congressional
limitations on its jurisdiction, the district court found
“implicit” procedural rights in statutes that did not
provide them, preventing the Trump Administration
from employing reasonable procedures for enforcing
our nation’s immigration laws as written.

12
STATEMENT
The district court judge has issued a truly
remarkable set of injunctions, class certifications,
clarifications, threats of contempt, orders to nonparty
Government entities, and other rulings and
statements, seeking to rewrite the nation’s
immigration laws from a district court bench in
Boston.  The district court judge responsible was
nominated by President Biden in March 2024, reported
from committee on a party line vote, and confirmed
without a single Republican Senator voting aye.   He
received his judicial commission on December 6, 2024,
not long before he was assigned this case in March
2025.  Northeastern University Law School
constitutional law professor Jeremy R. Paul explained
the reality of President Biden’s appointment of district
judges (termed “Biden judges”), including this
particular district court judge:
The Democratic president’s federal court
nominees will “make a huge difference in a
variety of cases during the Trump
administration....”  “There will be a
tremendous amount of litigation during the
[incoming] administration....”  “Because of
Biden judges, there will be a lot of initial
victories [at the district court level].”
[John Micek, “Biden tapped a former
Worcester public defender as a federal judge.
Why it matters,” MassLive (Dec. 10, 2024)
(emphasis added).]

13
The Chief Justice has stated correctly:  “We do not
have Obama judges or Trump judges, Bush judges or
Clinton judges.”12  However, it appears that not all
judges have received that memo.  It is becoming
apparent to the American People that there are certain
judges who believe that their office gives them the
authority to defy both the President and Congress, as
they act, even though Congress expressly has denied
them authority, to prevent the immigration
enforcement changes which the People elected the
current Administration to put into effect.  The First
Circuit has declined repeatedly to restore order, and
therefore, this is a matter that, again, requires
corrective action by this Court.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
The Statement of the Case, supra, demonstrates
what can happen when lower federal courts
circumvent statutory limitations on their jurisdiction
to assume control over and micromanage our nation’s
immigration policies.  This is particularly dangerous
when the immigration policies intersect with foreign
policy, as they do when the issue is removal to third
countries.
Section I, infra, explains how the district court’s
injunctive and declaratory relief provided not just to
the Plaintiffs-Appellees, but to a broad class, violate
the text of not one, but multiple different congressional
limitations on the powers of lower federal courts.  The
12  Mark Sherman, “Roberts, Trump spar in extraordinary scrap
over judges,” AP (Nov. 21, 2018).

14
courts below were so hostile to the notion that they
could be limited in giving relief to illegal aliens
awaiting removal that it is easy to get the impression
that they believe they could circumvent such
restrictions at will.  As a result, Section II, infra, reasserts the basis for the power of Congress to limit the
authority of the lower federal courts.
Section III, infra, analyzes the manner in which
the lower courts manufactured “due process” rights for
illegal aliens, finding them “implicit” in the very
statutes which empower the federal government to
remove them expeditiously.  Lastly, Section IV, infra,
shows the danger of allowing federal courts to meddle
in removal procedures, especially where it involves our
nation’s foreign policy and national security involving
removals of illegal aliens to foreign countries.
ARGUMENT
I. THE DISTRICT COURT ACTED ULTRA
VIRES IN VIOLATING MULTIPLE
CONGRESSIONAL LIMITATIONS ON
FEDERAL COURT JURISDICTION.

The courts below worked hard to find a rationale
to evade restrictions imposed by multiple
congressional limitations on federal court jurisdiction
set out in 8 U.S.C. section 1252, designed to govern
“Judicial review of orders of removal.”  That section
contains four separate limitations on federal court
jurisdiction over removals, and the district and circuit
courts manufactured a path around each.  This amicus
lacks the resources, and the space, to address the cases

15
which the lower court believes support their
interpretation of these statutes, and therefore will only
offer an analysis of the text.
In reviewing how the lower courts rationalized
their own authority, the following question should be
kept in mind.  Assuming Congress really wanted to
severely restrict judicial review of matters involving
removal of illegal aliens, is there any language
Congress could have used that these particular lower
courts would have found sufficient to divest them of
the judicial power to do what they wanted to do?
A. 8 U.S.C. section 1252(g).
First, 8 U.S.C. section 1252(g), entitled “Exclusive
jurisdiction,” states that unless otherwise provided:
no court shall have jurisdiction to hear
any cause or claim by or on behalf of any alien
arising from the decision or action by the
Attorney General to [i] commence proceedings,
[ii] adjudicate cases, or [iii] execute removal
orders against any alien under this Act.  [8
U.S.C. § 1252(g) (emphasis added).]
The circuit court understood the district court to have
ruled that this limitation only applied to prosecutorial
discretion over individual removal decisions, not policy
changes that govern many individual such challenges.
See D.V.D. V at *18.  The circuit court agreed with this
view because, inter alia, “[r]emoval orders are not
mere directives that noncitizens be removed [but] must

16
‘identify a country...’ [and] [t]he class does not contest
its removability....”  Id. at *19.
The lower courts’ interpretation reads language
into the statute, and leads to several irrational results.
First, there is no statutory language on which these
courts base their reading of the statute to restrict the
limitation on review to matters of “prosecutorial
discretion.”  Second, these courts would allow a group
of plaintiffs, such as the four illegal aliens13 here, to
challenge individual removal orders en masse, when
they clearly could not bring such challenges
individually.  Under this interpretation, all that an
immigration rights lawyer would need to do to
challenge enforcement decisions is to join claims by
two or more illegal aliens being removed.  Third, this
reading gives a peculiarly narrow meaning and effect
to the statutory phrase “arising from,” so that a claim
by an alien to the decision to remove that alien does
not “aris[e] from the decision or action” to remove
that alien.  As the Government argues, a “claim about
where an alien will be removed is, ipso facto, a ‘claim’
‘arising from the decision or action’ to ‘execute [a]
removal order[].’ 8 U.S.C. 1252(g).”  Pet. Br. at 16
(emphasis added).
13  The circuit court follows the lead of the Plaintiffs-Appellees,
never once referring to Plaintiffs as illegal aliens, and never even
using the “politically correct” term “undocumented” aliens.

17
B. 8 U.S.C. section 1252(b)(9).
Section 1252(b) governs “Requirements for review
of orders of removal.”  It provides, in relevant part, the
following requirements for review of an order of
removal:
Judicial review of all questions of law and
fact, including interpretation and
application of constitutional and
statutory provisions, arising from any
action taken or proceeding brought to remove
an alien from the United States under this
title ... shall be available only in judicial
review of a final order under this section.
Except as otherwise provided in this section,
no court shall have jurisdiction, by habeas
corpus ... or by any other provision of law
(statutory or nonstatutory), to review such an
order or such questions of law or fact.
[8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(9) (emphasis added).]
The rather clear language of this section was likewise
disregarded on the theory that “this is not a case that
seeks review of an order of removal, the decision to
seek removal, or the process by which removability is
determined.”  D.V.D. V at *30.  Again, Congress uses
the broad language “arising from” to describe its scope
of claims to which it applies, described as “any action
taken or proceeding brought to remove a alien....”
Again, one must ask, if Congress really wanted to limit
judicial review, what language would have been
deemed sufficient by the lower courts.  Again, the
answer would appear to be none.

18

II. THE COURTS BELOW DEFIED THE
AUTHORITY OF CONGRESS TO LIMIT THE
JURISDICTION OF THE LOWER FEDERAL

The district court also rebels against Congress’s
decision to place review of administrative alien
removal decisions only in the federal Courts of
Appeals, and the power “to enjoin or restrain” their
operation of  injunctive remedy only in this Court.
The district court made its disapproval of the law clear
by quoting a First Circuit case for the proposition that
the actual physical removal of an alien is “‘wholly
collateral to, the removal process,’ not ‘arising from’ it.”
D.V.D. III at 371.  In the district court’s view, once a
removal order is entered, anything else relating to the
actual removal is reviewable.  Although the court is
entitled to disagree with Congress’s decision, it is not
entitled to ignore it or evade it.
It is beyond question that Congress can limit the
jurisdiction of a district court.  Article III states, “The

22
judicial Power of the United States, shall be vested in
one supreme Court, and in such inferior Courts as the
Congress may from time to time ordain and establish.”
U.S. Const. Art. III.  In 1789, Congress passed, and
President Washington signed, the Judiciary Act of
1789, which created the first lower federal courts,
including district courts, and outlined the limits of
their jurisdiction.15  “[T]he Circuit Courts were created
by an act of Congress, and they are not authorized to
exercise jurisdiction in any case except where the
jurisdiction was conferred by an act of Congress.”
United States v. Eckford, 73 U.S. 484, 488 (1868).
Jurisdictional limitations are not new, nor are they
untested in this Court.  In 1869, in Ex Parte McCardle,
this Court recognized Congress’s power under Article
III to strip it of appellate jurisdiction.  William
McCardle, a newspaper publisher, printed articles
critical of the Reconstruction program and was jailed
by the military.  He applied for a writ of habeas corpus
with a federal district court, and the case was appealed
to this Court.  Fearful that the Court would strike
down the Reconstruction program, Congress passed a
law stripping this Court of appellate jurisdiction over
habeas appeals.  In McCardle, this Court properly
acknowledged Congress’s power to strip it of
jurisdiction and conceded it had no jurisdiction to hear
McCardle’s appeal.  Ex Parte McCardle, 74 U.S. 506
(1869).

Nor is McCardle an outlier.  This Court recognized
the principle again a half-century later for the lower
courts:
Only the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court is
derived directly from the Constitution.  Every
other court created by the general
government derives its jurisdiction
wholly from the authority of Congress.
That body may give, withhold or restrict
such jurisdiction at its discretion,
provided it be not extended beyond the
boundaries fixed by the Constitution....  The
Constitution simply gives to the inferior courts
the capacity to take jurisdiction in the
enumerated cases, but it requires an act of
Congress to confer it....  And the jurisdiction
having been conferred may, at the will of
Congress, be taken away in whole or in
part....  [Kline v. Burke Constr. Co., 260 U.S.
226, 234 (1922) (emphasis added).]
Even more recently, this Court stated:  “There can
be no question of the power of Congress thus to define
and limit the jurisdiction of the inferior courts of the
United States.”  Lauf v. E. G. Shinner & Co., 303 U.S.
323, 330 (1938).  In 1943, this Court repeated the
principle, this time citing an array of past cases.
The Congressional power to ordain and
establish inferior courts includes the power “of
investing them with jurisdiction either limited,
concurrent, or exclusive, and of withholding
jurisdiction from them in the exact degrees

24
and character which to Congress may
seem proper for the public good.”
[Lockerty v. Phillips, 319 U.S. 182, 187 (1943)
(emphasis added) (citations omitted).]
This Court has recognized Congress’s authority to
limit lower court jurisdiction as expressly sourced in
the Constitution.
To deny this position would be to elevate
the judicial over the legislative branch of
the government, and to give to the former
powers limited by its own discretion
merely.  It follows, then, that the courts
created by statute must look to the statute as
the warrant for their authority; certainly
they cannot go beyond the statute, and
assert an authority with which they may
not be invested by it, or which may be
clearly denied to them....  The existence of
the Judicial Act itself ... furnishes proof
unanswerable on this point.  The courts of the
United States are all limited in their nature
and constitution, and have not the powers
inherent in courts existing by prescription or
by the common law.  [Cary v. Curtis, 44 U.S.
236, 245 (1845) (superseded by statute on
other grounds) (emphasis added).]
Nor is Congress the only branch to recognize this
authority.  Indeed:
[w]hen Chief Justice John Roberts was Special

IV. THE CASE BELOW ILLUSTRATES THE
UNWORKABLE FOLLY OF “FOREIGN
POLICY BY JUDGE.”
The Statement of the Case section of an appellate
brief is often useful primarily to provide the posture of
the case as it comes to an appellate court.  This case is
an exception, and this amicus has attempted to set out
a detailed Statement of the Case which reveals the
impossibility of the Department of Homeland Security
enforcing our nation’s immigration laws while being
directed by a federal district court judge who appears
committed to preserving the status quo.  And of all
immigration laws, the removal of illegal aliens to a
third country requires “delicate diplomatic
negotiations with third countries to accept these
aliens.... [and] ‘significant logistical difficulties’ to

31
coordinate flights, pilots, crews, country clearances,
and foreign law-enforcement across multiple
countries.”  Pet. Br. at 11.  Thus, every such removal
involves the conduct of our nation’s foreign policy.
Although federal law provides guidance on where the
illegal alien is sent, in the end, it entrusts the matter
to the Department of Homeland Security — not a
district court.
The course of proceedings below reveals how
severely the lower courts impeded the Executive
Branch in carrying out its duties under immigration
law.   The district court granted motion after motion
filed by Plaintiffs to protect illegal aliens from the
consequences of their illegal acts, while giving no
deference to the branch of government entrusted with
the duty to remove illegal aliens.  If this type of
judicial intervention is permitted, the work of DHS
will be put on hold as the Justice Department will be
required to respond on short notice, or no notice, to a
bevy of motions and orders entered ultra vires.
On the immigration front, the human costs have
already been incalculable.  As immigration officials
have scrambled to keep up with the orders of hostile
judicial micro-managers, the worst-of-the-worst violent
criminal aliens have gamed the system, escaping back
into the general population, sometimes for years, to
commit still more heinous crimes against Americans.
See Pet. Br. at 3.
Not surprisingly, as the Government points out,
many of these criminal aliens’ countries of origin were
happy to unload their worst criminals on America and

32
are usually unwilling to take them back.  “As a result,
criminal aliens are often allowed to stay in the United
States for years on end, victimizing law-abiding
Americans in the meantime.”  App. Stay I at 2.  As a
result of the open borders policy pursued by prior
Administrations which refused to follow federal law,
now DHS has been given the task of finding a “third
country” willing to take these hard cases at all — then
hope that nation doesn’t change its mind while a
district court judge usurps Executive Branch
authority, disrupting “delicate diplomatic negotiations
that would be undermined by lengthy delays.”  Pet. Br.
at 3.
Congress recognized that “[s]uch delicate and
difficult judgments about international relations fall
beyond the judicial ken.”  Does v. Taliban, 101 F.4th 1,
12 (D.C. Cir. 2024).  Moreover, they defy a judicial
timeline.  Foreign policy judgments such as these
cannot be subjected to briefing schedules imposed by
any of 400 federal district judges serving in 94 district
courts.  That is why such “difficult and complex
[questions] in international affairs ... are committed to
the Legislature and the Executive, not the Judiciary.”
Zivotofsky v. Kerry, 576 U.S. 1, 5 (2015).  The judiciary
is wholly unprepared to handle such matters.  As a
practical matter, decisions like the one below make
conduct of foreign policy impossible.  If not stopped by
this Court, the problem will spread as other federal
courts will believe themselves empowered to run our
nation’s foreign policy whenever a suit is filed.
The public confidence in the federal judiciary is at
an all-time low, in the wake of one of “the largest”

33
drops in confidence “Gallup has ever measured.”18
When the public realizes that the policy changes for
which they elected a President can be thwarted for
years by a single federal district judge, they will
realize they have “ceased to be their own rulers,” and
that confidence will sink further.  It is up to this Court
to restore the rule of law by reining in this pattern of
judicial excess.
